extraction.name: CADS
extraction.description: CADS is an open-source framework and large-scale dataset for whole-body CT anatomy segmentation, comprising 22,022 CT volumes with annotations for 167 anatomical structures spanning from head to knee across 40 diverse data sources and 16 countries.
extraction.creator: Murong Xu, Tamaz Amiranashvili, Fernando Navarro, Maksym Fritsak, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, Suprosanna Shit, Bastian Wittmann, Sezgin Er, Sebastian M. Christ, Ezequiel de la Rosa, Julian Deseoe, Robert Graf, Hendrik Möller, Anjany Sekuboyina, Jan C. Peeken, Sven Becker, Giulia Baldini, Johannes Haubold, Felix Nensa, René Hosch, Nikhil Mirajkar, Saad Khalid, Stefan Zachow, Marc-André Weber, Georg Langs, Jakob Wasserthal, Mehmet Kemal Ozdemir, Andrey Fedorov, Ron Kikinis, Stephanie Tanadini-Lang, Jan S. Kirschke, Stephanie E. Combs, Bjoern Menze
extraction.rai:dataCollection: CT scans were aggregated from over 40 diverse sources including large-scale public archives (TotalSegmentator, NLST, CT-RATE, AbdomenCT-1K), specialized collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI) and TCIA studies, plus newly contributed clinical acquisitions (484 head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 triphasic abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Physical data collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Approximately 79% of the initial collection (17,327 of 22,022 scans) lacked manual annotations, with only 4,695 (21%) containing partial annotations from public sources. Specific structures also varied in visibility or availability due to different fields of view or cropping.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Computed Tomography (CT) volumes covering whole-body, head-and-neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, and spine.
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: To generate dense 3D per-slice annotations from the SAROS dataset's sparse slice-based 2D annotations (available only every fifth axial slice), interpolation was performed between the annotated slices.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (sigma = 5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure identity while preserving anatomical structural integrity near the face area.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were standardized through a three-step pipeline: (1) reorientation to standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention, (2) resampling to a uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution, and (3) simplifying original affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear. For model training, intensities were scaled from the 5th to 95th percentiles to [0, 1] and clipped.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were developed through a multi-stage pseudo-labeling framework: (1) training specialized nnU-Net models on initial ground truth across 9 anatomical groups to propagate pseudo-labels across the entire dataset; (2) shape-informed label quality control using an auto-decoder based on implicit neural representations to score pseudo-labels and exclude the lowest-scoring 10%; (3) multi-strategy label generation combining GT-flavor, Pseudo-flavor, and Shape-flavor models ranked statistically per organ using Dice and HD95; (4) sequential label assembly with progressive merging based on reliability, where original ground truth takes highest priority; (5) post-processing refinements including brain centroid-based cropping to mitigate hallucinations and tubular structure detection via vesselFM to retrieve costovertebral joints in ribs. In addition, manual annotations of critical OARs were contributed for the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Statistical testing was conducted to determine the best model flavor per structure using Shapiro-Wilk test for normality, Levene's test for variance equality, followed by ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA, or Kruskal-Wallis tests, and post-hoc comparisons (Tukey's HSD or Dunn's test) with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. A detailed manual review of 65 TotalSegmentator test scans was performed by medical professionals to detect mislabeling between adjacent structures, missing segments, and over-segmentations, establishing a curated test set.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Three in-house medical research assistants and a clinical radiation oncologist (Jan C. Peeken) with 5.5 years in practice.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net, vesselFM, ANTs (Advanced Normalization Tools), and MIM software
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Newly acquired hospital head CT scans included facial features (blurred with Gaussian filtering to preserve privacy) from patients aged >= 18 years; general patient pathology and diagnostic data were included.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Aims to make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers, improve automated volume delineation of organs-at-risk for accelerated radiotherapy treatment planning, and enhance medical AI robustness in radiology.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The shape-based quality assessment excludes the lowest-scoring 10% of pseudo-labels, potentially eliminating atypical anatomical variations and pathological edge cases from the training set. Certain anatomical structures have extreme class imbalances (e.g., uppermost cervical vertebrae C1-C5 or buccal mucosa appearing in fewer scans).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Exclusion of low-quality segmentations in shape assessment may remove valid pathological edge cases; coverage is limited from head to knees (excluding hands and feet); the brain mask includes all central nervous components within the skull; optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; heart segmentation omits superior portions; rectum appears shorter than anatomical extent; trachea is limited to air content; facial features are anonymized restricting facial analysis.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Automatic multi-organ whole-body CT segmentation, radiation therapy treatment planning (OAR contouring), anatomical landmark detection, cross-modality registration, and opportunistic body composition analysis.
